paras: The Clive whitecap attacks were night attacks and threats in August 1903 against the Black residents of Clive, Iowa, a village a few miles west of Des Moines, by unidentified men the press called whitecaps. After an attempt to burn a house and the dynamiting of Isaac Anderson's home, notices ordered Black residents to leave and warned white employers not to hire them. No one was reported hurt and no arrest appears in the coverage, but the story ran from New York to the Dakotas, and the Iowa State Bystander, a Black weekly, read it as a sign that lynching was spreading north.

Clive lay five or six miles west of Des Moines on the Milwaukee railroad. The Bystander's editor, who interviewed Black and white residents, counted fewer than a dozen Black families there, all owning "nice homes and some very valuable land," and said none had ever been arrested. Anderson was a section hand on the Milwaukee road and, according to the Omaha Bee, had recently moved a small frame house from Des Moines to Clive.

About two weeks before the dynamiting, someone tried to burn a house: Anderson's, according to the wire, or, according to the Bystander, the former Chas. Richardson house, where his son Elmer lived alone and was away that night. The Bystander said the door had been soaked with coal oil and neighbors put out the blaze.

Around 2 a.m. one night the following week, about August 22 by the wire's count, dynamite went off under Anderson's house. The Bystander said the charge ran the full length of the house but destroyed only part of it. The wire reported the chimney and part of the walls shattered and the family "barely escaping with their lives," whereas the Omaha Bee described a small charge under one corner.

That night, the Bystander reported, a card was tacked up warning "All negroes" to "git" and white men who employed them that they were "liable to have 'something happen' to them." Unsigned letters warned former state representative Chas. Steward, Milwaukee section boss Mr. Olesen and a Mr. Kirk to hire no more Black workers.

The Bystander reported that the "better element of whites" were indignant and were helping Black residents look for the perpetrators. Benjamin J. Shepard, a Clive farmer whose brother-in-law's home had been dynamited, said he was not scared and believed some white men wanted to frighten Black owners into selling their homes cheap. No report of an arrest, indictment or trial was found in coverage that ends in early September.

White papers first carried the story on August 25, in a Des Moines dispatch headed "Warn Negroes to Leave" in the New York Sun and a brief in the Minneapolis Journal. The Omaha Bee's correspondent called it "an organized effort to drive colored men out of the town." A rewrite headed "Negroes in Terror" ran August 26 to 28 in Bismarck, Bemidji, Jamestown and Milbank, and the Rock Island Argus used "Race Question to Front in Iowa." These versions spelled the town "Cleve" or "Olive" and named the attackers only as "supposed" whitecaps.

By September the story had shrunk to digest lines, and the Black Hills Union ran it under the subhead "Colored Man at Clive Causes Indignation Among Citizens." The True Northerner of Paw Paw, Michigan, used the unnamed Iowa town to argue that "Violence cannot solve the problem," while attributing lynchings to crimes to which it said Black people "as a race seem inclined."

The Bystander gave the attacks much of its August 28 front page, adding the card's text, the letters to employers and the Richardson fire. Its editorial called the attackers "cowardly villains" more dangerous than anarchists, urged life imprisonment or hanging, and warned that "white capism, 'Tillmanism, mobism and lynching is fast speeding to the north."

Accounts differ on which house was set afire, how large the charge was and how many Black people lived in Clive; the wire said "several hundred." On each point the Bystander, whose editor visited Clive, gave the more detailed local version.

accounts.label: Des Moines wire report
accounts.gist: Supposed whitecaps posted notices warning the colored population to leave; Anderson's house was dynamited two nights before Aug. 24, shattering the chimney and part of the walls, and his home had been the target of a burning attempt two weeks earlier; the colored population of several hundred was terror-stricken.

accounts.label: Omaha Bee correspondent
accounts.gist: Anderson, a section hand who had recently moved a small frame house to Clive, was the victim of an organized effort to drive colored men out; a small charge under one corner blew off part of the chimney.

accounts.label: Black Hills Union wire version
accounts.gist: After a futile effort to dynamite Anderson's barn and home, supposed White Caps posted notices warning the colored population to flee; trouble was feared.

accounts.label: Iowa State Bystander (local Black weekly)
accounts.gist: Dynamite placed under the full length of I. J. Anderson's house went off about 2 a.m. and destroyed part of it; two weeks earlier someone soaked the door of the former Richardson house with coal oil and set it afire; the card and letters to employers followed the dynamiting.

accounts.label: Benjamin J. Shepard, Black resident
accounts.gist: The attackers were worse than anarchists; he believed some white men wanted to frighten Black owners into selling their homes cheap.

framing.detail: Headlines such as 'Warn Negroes to Leave', 'Negroes in Terror' and 'Race Question to Front in Iowa' presented the notices and dynamiting without comment on the perpetrators beyond 'supposed whitecaps'.
The Omaha Bee's correspondent called it 'an organized effort to drive colored men out of the town' under the headline 'Colored Men Are Warned'.
The Black Hills Union headed the wire 'Colored Man at Clive Causes Indignation Among Citizens'.

The True Northerner's editorial held that 'Violence cannot solve the problem' and that Black citizens had property rights, while attributing lynchings to crimes to which it said Black people 'as a race seem inclined'.
The Bystander called the attackers 'cowardly villains' more dangerous than anarchists, urged life imprisonment or hanging, and warned that white capism and lynching were 'fast speeding to the north'.
